reason: The provided sources give a complete, multi-site verified account of Betelgeuse's 2019 Great Dimming, its surface mass ejection, and its eventual supernova fate.
story: In late 2019, skywatchers noticed something shocking: Betelgeuse, the glowing red supergiant marking Orion's shoulder, was rapidly fading. By February 2020, the giant star had lost nearly two-thirds of its normal brightness, dropping out of the top ten brightest stars in the night sky. Speculation erupted across the world that Betelgeuse was about to detonate in a dramatic supernova. But space observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope soon uncovered the true culprit. A superhot bubble of plasma had erupted from a giant convection cell on the star's surface, launching a massive plume of material millions of miles into space. As this ejected gas expanded into space, it cooled into a dense cloud of dust that blocked starlight from a quarter of Betelgeuse's surface. By April 2020, the cloud dissipated and the star returned to normal, reassuring astronomers that its eventual supernova is still up to 100,000 years away.
angle: Betelgeuse suddenly lost two-thirds of its light in 2019 because it blew out a massive plasma cloud that cooled into dust and blocked its own starlight.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star located in the constellation Orion.
If Betelgeuse were placed at the center of the solar system, its outer surface would extend past the orbit of Jupiter.
Starting in late 2019, Betelgeuse underwent a sudden drop in brightness known as the Great Dimming.
By mid-February 2020, Betelgeuse had lost roughly two-thirds of its normal visual brightness.
The rapid fading sparked media and public speculation that Betelgeuse was about to explode as a supernova.
Betelgeuse dropped from being one of the top ten brightest stars in the sky to outside the top twenty.
Observations by the Hubble Space Telescope revealed that the star ejected a massive plume of superhot material from its surface.
As the ejected material traveled millions of miles away from the star, it cooled and condensed into a cloud of starlight-blocking dust.
By April 2020, Betelgeuse had returned to its normal range of brightness.
Before the outburst, Betelgeuse had a regular pulsation brightness cycle of roughly 400 days.
Astronomers estimate Betelgeuse will explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years.
When Betelgeuse detonates as a supernova, life on Earth will remain unharmed due to its distance.
When the supernova occurs, it will shine as bright as a half-Moon for over three months.
The eventual supernova will be bright enough to be visible from Earth during the daytime.
Astrophysicist Andrea Dupree led Hubble Space Telescope studies analyzing the outburst on Betelgeuse.
Astrophysicist Miguel Montargès led observations of Betelgeuse using the Very Large Telescope in Chile during the dimming.

disputed: Distance to Betelgeuse: Sources cite varying distances including 410-548 light-years (S1, S4, S7) and 720-725 light-years (S2, S5, S6). Script handling: Attribute or state generally as around 500 to 700 light-years away.

Sole cause of dimming: Hubble studies emphasize dust condensation from a mass ejection (S2, S7), while other studies cite a large cool dark starspot (S4, S6). Script handling: Present the dust cloud from ejected gas as the primary Hubble finding while noting localized surface cooling also contributed.
